title: Log analysis
description: Reading the logs an analyst meets every day - Windows events, Linux authentication, web server, firewall, DNS and proxy logs - recognising normal from suspicious in each, and writing precise queries across them, ending with a hands-on log analysis lab on the course dataset.

lessons.title: Windows event analysis
lessons.summary: How to analyse Windows Security events rather than just recognise them: a seven-step reading method, actor-versus-target field reading, normal and suspicious patterns per event family, the four shapes of failed logons, and a worked analysis of the Banyan WS-104 chain with dwell gaps and absence checks.
objectives: Apply a repeatable method (question, inventory, baseline, deviation, chain, absence, context) to a Windows alert
Distinguish the actor from the target in 4624, 4720, 4732 and 1102 events
Classify groups of failed logons as typing errors, stale credentials, brute force or password spraying
Reconstruct and interpret an event chain on one host using dwell gaps and peer baselines
State accurately what the absence of an event does and does not show

lessons.title: Linux auth logs
lessons.summary: Reading Linux authentication logs in auth.log, secure and the journal: the anatomy of a syslog line, how one SSH login appears across sshd, PAM and systemd-logind, sudo and account-tool lines, separating internet noise from targeted guessing, and a worked analysis of an illustrative compromised server.
objectives: Interpret sshd, PAM, sudo, su, logind and account-tool lines field by field
Reconstruct an SSH session using the sshd PID and the logind session number
Separate background SSH noise from targeted guessing and from a success after failures
Extract failures, successes, sudo commands and account changes with grep, awk and journalctl
Identify the limits of auth.log evidence, such as SSH keys written as files

lessons.title: Web server logs
lessons.summary: How to read web server access and error logs as an analyst: the Combined Log Format field by field, status codes and response sizes, client addresses behind proxies and self-declared user agents, and how to recognise content discovery, path traversal and injection attempts and judge from the server's answer whether they succeeded, while ruling out benign look-alikes.
objectives: Interpret each field of a Combined Log Format access-log line and of an nginx error-log line
Explain what each HTTP status class reveals about how far a suspicious request reached
Recognise content discovery, path traversal and injection attempts in encoded request lines
Distinguish scanning and injection attempts from crawlers, health checks, authorised scans and ordinary user input
Analyse an access log with command-line counts to reconstruct one source's activity and decide the next action

lessons.title: Firewall logs
lessons.summary: How to analyse firewall logs: stateful logging of decisions, drop versus reject, netfilter and session-log fields, tracing a host through source NAT, and recognising vertical scans, horizontal sweeps, blocked outbound attempts, beacons, large transfers and out-of-state drops against their benign look-alikes.
objectives: Interpret netfilter log lines and next-generation firewall session records field by field
Explain how state tracking, logging configuration and drop or reject actions shape what a firewall records
Trace an external report about the public address back to an internal host through NAT session logs
Identify port scans, sweeps, blocked outbound attempts and beaconing from counts of ports, hosts, intervals and bytes
Separate suspicious connection patterns from background scanning, update traffic, backups and expired sessions

lessons.title: DNS logs
lessons.summary: How to read DNS resolver, sensor and endpoint DNS records, what normal DNS looks like, and how NXDOMAIN bursts, long high-entropy labels, many unique subdomains, TXT volume and resolver bypass reveal domain generation algorithms and DNS tunnelling from the defender's side.
objectives: Interpret the fields of a DNS query record and pivot from name, answer and timestamp to other evidence
Explain how recursive resolution carries a query name to the zone's authoritative server and why that enables DNS tunnelling
Recognise DGA, tunnelling and resolver-bypass patterns and distinguish them from their benign look-alikes
Evaluate Shannon entropy and rarity as detection features using real output from the lab domains
Design DNS logging and egress controls that make resolver logs complete

lessons.title: Proxy logs
lessons.summary: A method for analysing web proxy logs: record anatomy and field pitfalls, what TLS inspection changes, and a six-question workflow (rarity, content, rhythm, volume, scope, endpoint pivot) applied with minisiem.py and hunt.py to the WS-104 beacon and upload in the lab dataset.
objectives: Interpret proxy log fields, including byte direction, status-code origin and CONNECT records
Compare the evidence available with and without TLS inspection
Apply rarity, content, rhythm, volume and scope queries to proxy data with minisiem.py and hunt.py
Build a source-cited case timeline joining proxy and endpoint events
State conclusions from proxy evidence at the strength the evidence supports

lessons.title: Query writing
lessons.summary: Turning an analytical question into a precise, tested query: specification, type-safe and anchored conditions, half-open time ranges, grain, bounded joins, anti-joins and window functions, with real SQL on the Banyan dataset and SPL/KQL equivalents.
objectives: Write a query specification (population, condition, grain, window, output) from an analytical question
Avoid false and missed matches caused by types, substrings, time boundaries and NULLs
Write bounded joins and NULL-safe anti-joins without fan-out errors
Use CTEs, time buckets and window functions such as LAG() to compare periods and measure intervals
Test a query against known positives and negatives and express its precision and recall

lessons.title: Log lab
lessons.summary: A guided multi-source analysis of the Banyan dataset: baseline Windows, endpoint, VPN and proxy logs separately, merge the exceptions into one timeline, run scope checks and write a findings note.
objectives: Baseline Windows Security, Sysmon, VPN and proxy events with aggregation queries
Classify exceptions in each source as noise, suspicious or unexplained, with evidence
Build a merged timeline joined on host, user, address and time
Run scope checks and record their negative results and limits
Write a findings note that separates facts, confidence, gaps and recommended actions
